query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, brittle failure emerges not from traditional chemical segregation or intermetallic precipitation, but from a dynamic process in which high strain rate deformation induces severe grain refinement. This increases the fraction of high‐angle grain boundaries and triple junctions that—owing to their inherently high interfacial energy—become prone to local amorphization and decohesion (cavitation), leading to brittle behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, initially coarse-grained, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi)
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled high strain rate deformation (such as sliding contact or rapid tensile loading) at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 400°–800°C) compared to a baseline condition at low strain rate and room temperature
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in environments that minimize oxidation (e.g., ultra-high vacuum or inert gas) to ensure that chemical effects like segregation remain negligible; temperature and strain rate conditions varied to promote or avoid dynamic grain refinement
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic grain refinement that creates a higher fraction of high-angle grain boundaries and triple junctions
generation.mechanism: Under high-strain rate conditions at elevated temperatures, the alloy undergoes rapid grain refinement. The resulting increase in high-energy boundaries and triple junctions facilitates local amorphization and decohesion (cavitation) even without chemical segregation. These microstructural changes reduce the effective toughness of the material, causing a transition from ductile to brittle behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial coarse-grained baseline under low-strain, room-temperature conditions, the high strain rate and intermediate temperature conditions will lead to observable grain refinement, increased high-angle grain boundary fraction, and microstructural evidence of decohesion (e.g., cavitation) at grain boundaries and triple junctions. This microstructural change correlates with a marked loss in toughness.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained, single-phase HEA deformed at low strain rates and room temperature, where ductile behavior is maintained with minimal grain refinement and no significant evidence of grain boundary decohesion
generation.boundary: This brittle transition is expected only within the range of temperatures and strain rates that are sufficient to promote dynamic grain refinement. At very low temperatures or strain rates below a critical threshold, the mechanisms leading to grain boundary decohesion may not be activated.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical strain rate and temperature thresholds for significant dynamic grain refinement and subsequent decohesion are uncertain. Additionally, any subtle effects from minor impurity segregation under various conditions remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the HEA with a coarse-grained, single-phase structure. Divide these into two groups. Deform one group at high strain rates and intermediate temperatures (e.g., 600°C) under ultra-high vacuum conditions, while deforming the control group at low strain rates at room temperature. After deformation, analyze both groups using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to assess grain size distribution, the fraction of high-angle grain boundaries, and evidence of interfacial decohesion or cavitation. Perform mechanical testing to measure toughness and ductility in both groups.
measurements: Detection of local amorphization and cavitation at grain boundaries/triple junctions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high strain rate, intermediate temperature samples do not show a significantly reduced grain size, increased high-angle grain boundary or triple junction fraction, or evidence of interfacial decohesion (e.g., cavitation) relative to the control—even if the mechanical toughness is reduced—then the hypothesis attributing brittle behavior to dynamic grain refinement and subsequent decohesion is falsified.

Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Although recent experimental measurements of HAGB energy with this same alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) exist, a comparison of this prediction is difficult. Measurements of grain boundary energy are sensitive to thermally-driven grain boundary segregation (and possibly phase separation) of impurities. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution.
